title: Lawrence and Hale as instruments in themselves
summary: Green says audiences roared at their new sounds and likens them to instruments, dancing a cappella with no accompaniment.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, how did the audiences respond to them?

Oh, my goodness, whew. You could -- you could hardly hear your ears, I mean when they finished something, because it was new, you see and see they educate the public, because the public at that time, they wanted to learn -- like if they see something that they'd like to have something -- I think it -- I can do that, and sitting in the audience. You know how one analyzes? You know? They would have to explain it when they left, someone asked them, where you been what did you do and so forth, they would have to explain what they did or what they saw, or something, it was interesting, you know, did you have a nice night, and so forth.
Well what was so different about their way of tapping? That hadn't -- the public hadn't seen?
It was one of a kind -- it was like an instrument. Like a trombone is not a trumpet. Like that.
In other words, what you're saying at this point in time, tap dancing had transcended the dance form and had become --

No, John I'm not saying tap dancing, I'm not saying the art, I'm saying these personalities, Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale -- they were one of a kind -- they didn't -- they wasn't like because they're tap dancers and that's a tap dancing -- that -- they're not in unison. See, they're different personalities of the art.
the dance form and made it an instrument within the band, rather than a dancer with a band, they were an instrument in the band.

They were a musical -- there was music. They were music, themselves. See, cause tap dancing is a material, you know like -- like they do -- they call it a capella -- that's what I -- that's without musical accompaniment, you see, accompaniments, you see? That's -- you just hear the tap dancers, you know, the tap and the -- and the floor, you see, that's what that is.

Now a lot of times audiences used to come in a place and Baby Lawrence and Teddy Hale would already be there. And they'd be up on the floor and there nobody playing a musical instrument. But you would hear them and a lot a -- of times, like the projectionist, you know, has got to come down, like turn the lights on -- so forth, you understand? But it was -- like say for instance you go to a great playground or recreation place, you know, and you -- you know, -- you never know, you may see like a Harlem Globetrotter out there somewhere playing at one of these places -- they teach -- you know, self-preservation, you see.
But I'm just saying, that audiences some of them were fortunate you know, say I remember when, they could say this --
